newsitem.title: USA: US foreign crudes scarce, North Sea imports costly.
newsitem.headline: US foreign crudes scarce, North Sea imports costly.

text.p: U.S. foreign crudes remained scarce and costly into the Gulf Coast but North Sea Brent was shown despite a largely shut arbitrage, traders said.
"Brent won't cut it against LLS (Light Louisiana Sweet), not even with Gulf sweets up at 60-70 cents premium," a Gulf Coast trader said, citing December domestic prices.
A major with a collection of about eight Brents was heard showing delivered Brent at a nominal level of Dec West Texas Intermediate plus 50 cents cif for end Nov/early Dec arrival.
But pipeline tariffs and freight costs were deemed prohibitive for Brent-related imports.
West African cargoes were also thin with an independent holding Qua Iboes for similar timing not yet showing numbers.
In nearby markets, waterborne availability was confined to one cargo of Oriente for late Nov with a value around WTI minus $2.60 cif, but interest was lukewarm, traders said.
A Canadon Seco cargo was also seen available to the U.S. although more likely to be moved to the West Coast.
Meanwhile, Canadian exports to U.S. northern tier refiners continued to flush out Gulf Coast sours.
The close of the asphalt production season and new growth in Canadian heavy oil drilling dampened demand in the spot market for Latin American as well as domestic barrels.
In the U.S. after-market, Brent intermonth spreads for Nov/Dec traded at 33 cents, and Dec/Jan at +58/59 cents, within the range seen during the earlier London session.
Dec Brent partials traded several times at $24.25 a barrel to a Wall Street trader.
